rows.verified: Isocyanates can be present in polyurethane paints, coatings, foams, glues and flooring products.
Spraying isocyanate products can create very high exposure because aerosol mist droplets are readily inhaled.
Risk assessment should identify who may be exposed, the product and isocyanate form, the application method and the degree of enclosure.
Prevention options include using products without isocyanates or less volatile forms and avoiding unnecessary spraying.
Spray work should use an enclosed area with local exhaust ventilation where practicable, with extracted air discharged safely.
HSE guidance specifies constant-flow air-fed breathing apparatus for isocyanate spraying and exclusion of non-essential people.
Sprayers should keep respiratory protection on until they have left the spraying area because mist clearance can take time.
HSE recommends biological monitoring for vehicle spray painters to check whether exposure controls are working effectively.
Isocyanate risk depends on product chemistry, volatility, application method, enclosure, ventilation, clearance time, respiratory protection and worker sensitisation.
Isocyanate guidance is product-, task-, exposure- and worker-specific and is not an exact parcel-level asthma probability.
Flour dust can irritate the eyes and nose, cause dermatitis and produce occupational asthma after sensitisation.
Flour dust is a hazardous substance controlled under COSHH.
Because flour dust is an asthmagen, exposure should be reduced as far below the workplace exposure limit as reasonably practicable.
Control measures include careful handling, dust extraction and vacuum or wet cleaning rather than dry sweeping.
HSE laboratory testing found low-dust flours reduced measured dust during manual sieving by approximately 47 to 86 percent compared with normal flour.
HSE testing found reductions of approximately 67 to 78 percent when low-dust flour was tipped into containers or dredgers.
HSE COSHH sheets describe extraction and good practice for bag opening, tipping and dough mixing.
Health surveillance is normally required where bakery workers remain exposed to flour dust capable of causing asthma or dermatitis.
Flour-dust risk depends on ingredient dustiness, tipping and mixing method, automation, extraction, cleaning practice, duration and worker sensitisation.
Bakery evidence is process-, ingredient-, task- and worker-specific and is not an exact parcel-level respiratory-disease probability.
